corrections.source_says: Set context_class to none under the supplied codebook, while retaining observational as the design_class and no as core eligibility. The paper measures vocabulary characteristics within essays and compares their group means over time; it does not score creativity, novelty, originality, or diversity/similarity across different applicants' outputs. The authors' homogenization interpretation can remain a screening note, but it does not supply the diversity outcome required for observational context by codebook Sections 1, 3, and 6. This is a codebook-scope correction, not a numerical transcription error.

corrections.source_says: Use none. TTR, Maas TTR, MTLD, HDD, and Yule's K describe vocabulary variety or repetition within an essay. Their temporal changes are not scores of creativity, novelty, originality, usefulness, or ideation, and they do not measure diversity between people. AI availability alone does not make these stylistic measures an eligible with_ai creativity outcome.

confirmed: Read the entire markdown conversion, including references and Appendices A-E, and checked the recorded numbers against the PDF. The source is the 21-page arXiv:2602.17791v1 [cs.CY], dated 19 Feb 2026; the title and five authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and PDF page count). No claim from the later proceedings version was needed.

The design is observational and core eligibility is no: admissions records were analyzed retrospectively, with no random assignment of people to AI assistance. Random sampling for detector development is not treatment assignment; randomized audits are proposed as future research (PDF p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2.1; p. 10, Section 6).

The main corpus is 81,663 applications/essays from the 2019-2020 through 2023-2024 cycles, not a reported count of distinct randomized or analyzed people. Leaving the main people counts null and recording 81,663 as output units is supported (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 13, Appendix A).
The post-GPT sample is N = 17,654, and the study treats the 2024 cycle as post-GPT and the 2020-2023 cycles as pre-GPT (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.2.3).

Table 1 reports N = 7,377 higher-SES and 3,249 lower-SES cases among applicants with detectable LLM usage in 2023-2024. The form's 10,626 output units equal the sum of those two printed Ns; 10,626 is a derived total, not a separately printed sample size or a count of randomized people (PDF p. 5, Table 1 and Section 4.1).
MTLD is lower SES 90.88 (19.79) versus higher SES 95.78 (21.39), difference -4.90 (-5.1%)***, t = -11.13, exactly as recorded (PDF p. 5, Table 1; p. 6, Section 4.1).
Yule's K is lower SES 112.00 (18.84) versus higher SES 108.42 (18.67), difference 3.58 (3.3%)***, t = 9.07, exactly as recorded (PDF p. 5, Table 1).

Unique word types are lower SES 306.21 (41.90) versus higher SES 319.84 (33.38), printed difference -13.64 (-4.3%)***, t = -17.89. The printed difference is correctly preserved without recomputing it from rounded means (PDF p. 5, Table 1).

TTR is lower SES 0.51 (0.04) versus higher SES 0.52 (0.04), printed difference 0.00 (-0.9%)***, t = -5.61. The apparently rounded-zero difference is printed that way; *** denotes p < 0.001 (PDF p. 5, Table 1 and its note).

Figure 1 supplies graphical group means with 95% confidence intervals and the convergence claim quoted in S1-O1, without a numerical test of the change in the group gap. Visual inspection confirms S1-O2's stated 2024 directions: TTR, MTLD, and HDD rise, while Maas TTR and Yule's K fall in both SES groups. The form also correctly flags the disagreement between the prose about lower-SES TTR in 2020 and the plotted ordering (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1; p. 6, Figure 1a-b).

The one-line finding correctly transcribes mean estimated LLM usage of 0.102 for lower-SES versus 0.080 for non-waiver applicants, and MTLD 90.88 versus 95.78; its convergence wording reproduces the authors' interpretation of Figure 1 (PDF p. 7, Section 4.2.1; p. 5, Table 1; p. 6, Figure 1).
The essays concern eight Common App prompts at a selective U.S. engineering school; essays under 250 words were excluded and the maximum was 650 words (PDF p. 13, Appendix A and Table 5).

GPT-4o generated the synthetic reference essays; actual applicant AI use was unobserved and estimated with an essay-level detector. The authors explicitly say the estimate does not identify individual LLM use as ground truth (PDF p. 3, Sections 3.2.1-3.2.2; p. 4, Section 3.2.2).

Appendices A-E are included in this PDF, with essay prompts, detector validation, assumption checks, stratified regressions, and mediation results as described. They add no randomized people study or measure of diversity across applicants' outputs. This is an original corpus analysis, not a synthesis, so there are no pooled creativity estimates to verify (PDF pp. 13-21, Appendices A-E; p. 3, Section 3).
summary: The arXiv version, corpus counts, and reported numerical results are accurate, and the paper contains no randomized people study. Four scope coding corrections are needed because within-essay vocabulary measures and convergence of group means do not meet the codebook's definitions of creativity or diversity across people's outputs.
